newsitem.title: UK: World oil prices fall as US inventories rise sharply.
newsitem.headline: World oil prices fall as US inventories rise sharply.

text.p: World oil prices fell on Wednesday after U.S. data suggested demand for crude and gasoline in the key North American market would fall.
Figures released by the American Petroleum Institute showed a hefty seven-million-barrel rise in crude stocks from the previous week and a startling 23-million- barrel year-on-year increase.
The numbers kicked benchmark Brent crude futures off two-month highs attained in a dizzying five-day rally which peaked on Monday.
The June Brent contract settled 12 cents down at $19.51 a barrel after trading around the $19.35 mark for most of the day.

The API statistics were regarded with scepticism by some market players, who pointed to internal contradictions in the numbers, but the market saturation they implied was at least partly backed by U.S. Department of Energy figures.
"The APIs and DOE confirmed each other, so you got to believe the data," said Victor Yu, vice-president at Refco Inc in New York.
The numbers looked equally gloomy for gasoline, the product that traditionally supports oil prices during the northern hemisphere's summer by sucking in imports from abroad.

API statistics showed a much larger than anticipated 6.5-million-barrel rise in gasoline stocks in the last week, suggesting there will be less import demand during the peak U.S. driving season than previously believed.
Crude's fall had been anticipated by many, who blamed the $2 hike in values over the last week on speculation and said it was contrary to the market's negative long-term outlook.

Oil supplies look set to greatly outstrip demand this summer, with members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries busting their output quotas, increased non-OPEC production and stagnating demand.

However, oil traders have clutched at straws to mark up prices in the last week, seeing short-term support in Gulf tension, tribal feuds blocking oil movement in Nigeria and North Sea maintenance programmes.

U.S. sabre-rattling over Iranian wargames in the Gulf is no longer a market factor and Shell Nigeria announced on Wednesday it was restarting oil pumps closed down on Sunday by a local dispute over the alleged diversion of relief aid.
Last week's rally began with rumours that maintenance would cut deeply into the number of North Sea crude cargoes in June.
First details of loading programmes partly bore out those worries but market players have in any case begun to discount the effect of the cargo cutbacks.

"I still think it (crude) is going to come off. The U.S. stock build is bearish and refiners have built up stocks here over the past few weeks. Fundamentally we are not looking good," one North Sea oil producer said.
The outlines of the more significant Brent and Forties June cargo programmes were expected on Thursday and should help set short-term trends.
"I'm bearish overall but there are worries about early June. That's why I'm interested in seeing the Forties schedule," said another producer.
